title: Why the Bat Hides by Day
subtitle: Why-stories and morals in Ogumefu's collection

bat.author: Yoruba storytellers; collected and published in English by M. I. Ogumefu
bat.translator: not applicable; authored in English by M. I. Ogumefu
bat.locator: Legend XI · THE BAT; Legend XI · THE BAT, normalized characters 11-676
bat.excerpt: THE Bat is half a bird and half a rodent, and lives partly on the earth and partly in the air, but both rats and birds shun him, and this is why: The rats, his cousins, were once fighting a great battle with the birds, and Bat fought in their midst. But when he saw that the birds were likely to be victorious, he left the rats and flew up into the air to fight on the side of the birds. Both the rats and the birds were disgusted at this cowardly action, so they ceased from fighting one another and all combined to attack the Bat. Since that day he has been forced to hide in dark places all day, and only comes out in the evening when his enemies cannot see him.
bat.note: Verbatim English text from M. I. Ogumefu's 1929 collection, which his preface describes as belonging to the Yoruba country of Southern Nigeria. It is a Yoruba-authored retelling for readers, not an ethnographic record of practice.

narrativeBlocks.title: A deserter in mid-battle
narrativeBlocks.body: In Ogumefu's tale, the Bat fights beside his cousins the rats, but when the birds begin to win he flies up and joins their side instead.

narrativeBlocks.title: Both armies turn on him
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (Yoruba Legends; whitespace normalized): “THE Bat is half a bird and half a rodent, and lives partly on the earth and partly in the air, but both rats and birds shun him, and this is why: The rats, his cousins, were once fighting a great battle with the birds, and Bat fought in their midst. But when he saw that the birds were likely to be victorious, he left the rats and flew up into the air to fight on the side of the birds. Both the rats and the birds were disgusted at this cowardly action, so they ceased from fighting one another and all combined to attack the Bat. Since that day he has been forced to hide in dark places all day, and only comes out in the evening when his enemies cannot see him.”

narrativeBlocks.title: A story that explains a habit
narrativeBlocks.body: Disgusted by his disloyalty, rats and birds unite against the Bat, who must now hide in dark places all day and only come out in the evening. The moral punishes a traitor; the ending explains a real animal's behaviour.

narrativeBlocks.title: The collector's own description
narrativeBlocks.body: Ogumefu writes in his 1929 preface that these legends “relate the adventures of men and animals, and try to explain the mysteries of Nature”, naming the leopard’s spots and women’s long hair as examples. In his leopard tale, every arrow the hunter Akiti fires leaves a dark mark on the Leopard’s coat; the Bat’s nights fit the same why-story pattern.

narrativeBlocks.title: Two jobs at once
narrativeBlocks.body: These tales explain an animal's feature (spots, night-flying) and judge a character's conduct (cowardice, greed) at the same time. Reading only the moral or only the explanation misses half the design.

quiz.prompt: Why do the rats and the birds unite against the Bat?

choices.text: He stole their food stores during the fight
He refused to take any side at all
He abandoned the rats mid-battle to join the winning side

quiz.explanation: The Bat fought with the rats but flew to the birds when they seemed to be winning; both armies, disgusted, joined to attack him.
